title: Shared Ancestor in Any Tree
statement:
You get the root of a binary tree whose values are all distinct, but are not ordered in any way: this is not a search tree. You also get two different values p and q, and both appear in the tree.

Return the value of their lowest shared ancestor: the deepest node that has both p and q in its subtree. A node counts as being in its own subtree, so if p is above q, the answer is p.

Trees are written in level order with null for a missing child.

examples.in: root = [8, 3, 6, 9, 1, null, 4, null, null, 7, 2], p = 7, q = 4
examples.why: 7 is deep in the left half and 4 is in the right half, so they only meet at the root. Steering by "smaller goes left" would wander down the left side, because the values are not ordered.

examples.in: root = [8, 3, 6, 9, 1, null, 4, null, null, 7, 2], p = 1, q = 2
examples.why: 2 is a child of 1, and 1 counts as its own ancestor. The answer is p itself.

examples.in: root = [8, 3, 6, 9, 1, null, 4, null, null, 7, 2], p = 9, q = 2
examples.why: 9 hangs on the left of 3 and 2 on the right of 3's child 1, so 3 is the lowest node holding both.

constraints: p ≠ q, and both are values in the tree
The tree is at most 500 levels deep
hints: Without ordering you cannot tell from a value which way to go. What could each subtree report back to its parent instead?

Let a recursive call return whether it found p or q in its subtree. The lowest node where both sides report something, or where the node itself is one target and a side reports the other, is the answer.
find(node): return null for null; return the node if its value is p or q; otherwise recurse both ways. If both sides return non-null, this node is the answer; else pass up whichever side is non-null.

explain.intuition:
In a search tree you could steer by comparing values. Here values say nothing about position, so you have to search. Do it bottom-up: ask each subtree "did you see p or q?" and let the answers flow up. The first node, coming up from the bottom, where the two answers arrive from different sides is where the paths to p and q split, which is the lowest shared ancestor.

The ancestor case falls out for free. When the search reaches p, it returns p at once without looking below it. If q is somewhere under p, nothing else in the tree reports q, so p travels all the way up as the answer, which is correct. It is the same idea as finding the nearest common parent of two DOM elements, except the DOM gives you parent pointers, and here you only have child links.
steps: Define find(node) returning a node or null.
If node is null, or its value is p or q, return node.
If both are non-null, p and q are on different sides: return node.
Otherwise return whichever of l, r is non-null. The answer is the value of find(root).
pitfalls: Steering by value as if it were a search tree. The first example breaks that immediately.
Continuing to search below p after finding it, and then reporting a deeper node. When one target is an ancestor of the other, the ancestor is the answer.
Returning true/false instead of the node. A boolean alone cannot tell the parent which node to report.

solutions.title: Parent links, then compare the two paths
solutions.idea: Walk the tree once to record every node's parent. Mark all ancestors of p, then climb from q until you hit a marked node.

solutions.title: Post-order: report finds upward
solutions.idea: Each call returns the target it found in its subtree, or null. The node where finds arrive from both sides is the answer.

followups: p or q might be missing from the tree. How do you report that instead of returning a wrong ancestor?
Each node also has a parent pointer, but you do not get the root. How does that turn into a linked-list problem?
lcTitle: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
